newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Montreal sees 1997 Canadian growth surge.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Montreal sees 1997 Canadian growth surge.

text.p: Bank of Montreal chief economist Tim O'Neill said on Monday he expects Canada's economy to surge in 1997 compared to 1996.

O'Neill told a group of reporters at the bank's economic outlook that if the government continues its current fiscal policy path of narrowing the deficit, gross domestic product should grow by about 3.4 percent on average from the fourth quarter of 1996 to the fourth quarter of 1997, compared to 1.3 percent annualized over the past two quarters.
He said the economy is expected to respond to low inflation and the fall in short-term interest rates.

"The interest rate-sensitive sectors, such as housing, have already begun to respond to the sharp decline in rates that has taken place since the spring of 1995. This, combined with continued solid gains in exports, should underpin strong economic growth by the fourth quarter of this year, and the momentum will continue through 1997," O'Neill said.
O'Neill said the current debate over a possible federal tax cut is inappropriate until the federal government has eliminated the nation's budget deficit.
"I think it is an inappropriate time to consider that," O'Neill said.

Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin projected on October 9 the 1998/99 budget deficit will narrow to C$9 billion or one percent of GDP from a 1996/97 projected deficit of C$24.3 billion or 3.0 percent of GDP.

O'Neill also said the Canadian dollar will benefit from the improved fundamentals and reduced political uncertainty to strengthen to 75 U.S. cents by late next year. However, the prospect of offsetting interest rate reductions from the Bank of Canada will limit gains.
He also said he expects the bank rate to fall an additional 25 basis points by early next year.

Long-term Canadian interest rates should continue to decline, with 10-year Government of Canada bonds yielding 6.0 percent by the last quarter of next year, down from 6.7 percent in the same period this year.
"The remarkable financial market story of 1996 is the dramatic downward shift in Canada's bond yields relative to those in the U.S," he said.
